cards.q: Why does bidirectionally redistributing between two protocols create routing loops?
cards.a: Redistributing in both directions across two protocols lets a route leave OSPF into EIGRP, come back into OSPF as an EIGRP external, and bounce again — inflating metrics and flapping the RIB. Prevention uses route tags, filters, AD tuning, and limited boundary routers.

cards.q: Describe the anatomy of a redistribution feedback loop.
cards.a: R1 redistributes OSPF to EIGRP (tag 100); R2 receives it in EIGRP and redistributes back into OSPF as an E1/E2; the route in OSPF now shows EIGRP as the external source, so metrics inflate, the table flaps, and the origin is wiped, possibly causing a blackhole.

cards.q: What are the defenses against redistribution loops and their relative strength?
cards.a: Route tags (tag at entry, deny the tag on the way back) are the strongest; filters (deny own prefixes at each boundary) are standard; a single boundary router is simplest; AD tuning is situational; and EIGRP stub/passive is supplemental.

cards.q: Describe the worked tag-based loop-prevention design.
cards.a: On the OSPF-to-EIGRP boundary, tag OSPF ranges with 'set tag 100' via route-map TAG-OSPF. On the EIGRP-to-OSPF boundary, use a route-map DENY-TAG-100 that denies tag 100 (then permits the rest) applied to 'redistribute eigrp 100 ... subnets' — so OSPF-originated routes never return to OSPF.

cards.q: What is the single-boundary-router rule for loop prevention?
cards.a: One ASBR between two domains eliminates the feedback pair entirely. Multi-boundary is only safe with symmetric filters plus tags on both routers.

cards.q: Can metric inflation occur even without a full loop in redistribution?
cards.a: Yes — even one-directional redistribution across two hops can inflate metrics, so ensure seed metrics are sensible so the return path stays stable.

cards.q: What are the symptoms that indicate a redistribution loop?
cards.a: Metric larger than expected (feedback re-advertisement), route flap between protocols (AD flip at the boundary), a route missing on one side (tag deny too broad), or BGP origin '?' everywhere (redistribute-based injection).

cards.q: Which commands detect and troubleshoot redistribution loops?
cards.a: 'show ip route <prefix>' watches metric growth, 'show ip eigrp topology' and 'show ip ospf database external' show E1/E2 tags, 'clear ip route *' after changes, and 'debug ip routing' traces flapping.

cards.q: What is the canonical loop-prevention answer on the exam?
cards.a: Tags at entry plus deny the tag at return — the tag-based loop defense is the canonical answer to a redistribution loop scenario.

cards.q: How does a single boundary router avoid redistribution loops entirely?
cards.a: With only one ASBR there is no feedback pair, because routes do not bounce between two independently redistributing boundary routers.

cards.q: What must multi-boundary loop-prevention designs do?
cards.a: Filter both directions symmetrically — apply matching filters and tags on both boundary routers so no direction lets routes return.

cards.q: What happens to a route's origin and metric when it gets caught in a redistribution loop?
cards.a: The loop wipes the origin — the route becomes external with an inflated metric.

cards.q: In the loop prevention quick review, what are the defenses and the best/worst designs?
cards.a: Route tag (tag entry, deny return), filter (deny own prefixes), single boundary (no feedback pair), AD tuning (stable winner), stub/passive (limit scope); detect via metric growth/flap; best answer is tag plus symmetric filter; worst is two-way blind redistribute.

cards.q: Why can a low-AD source survive a looped metric in a redistribution design?
cards.a: Because AD (note 05) beats metric: a low-AD source is preferred even when the metric has been inflated by a loop, so stable AD selection can mask the inflated metric.
